distillation_scope: Pure disease-name leaf distillation for the full clinical spectrum of Diabetic ketoacidosis. Euglycemic DKA, hyperosmolar overlap, SGLT2-inhibitor context, infection-triggered DKA, pregnancy, pancreatitis overlap, starvation or alcohol ketoacidosis mimics, and treatment complications are represented only as mechanisms, context axes, risk factors, treatment modifiers, or case evidence; they are not part of the disease name.

latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Insufficient effective insulin action from missed insulin, new autoimmune beta-cell failure, insulin pump failure, infection or stress hormones, SGLT2-inhibitor context, pregnancy, or severe insulin resistance. This is the initiating gate for DKA without forcing a subtype.

Glucagon, catecholamines, cortisol, growth hormone, infection, surgery, trauma, myocardial ischemia, vomiting, dehydration, and starvation physiology amplify hepatic glucose output, lipolysis, and ketogenesis.
Low insulin-to-glucagon signaling releases free fatty acids and drives hepatic beta-hydroxybutyrate and acetoacetate production, producing ketonemia, ketonuria, and high anion-gap metabolic acidosis.

Hepatic glucose output and reduced peripheral uptake usually produce hyperglycemia, glucosuria, polyuria, sodium-water loss, dehydration, and hyperosmolality. SGLT2 inhibitors, fasting, pregnancy, partial insulin treatment, or reduced intake can blunt glucose despite active ketoacidosis.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: High anion-gap acidemia and respiratory compensation
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Ketoacid accumulation consumes bicarbonate and lowers pH; respiratory compensation produces tachypnea or Kussmaul breathing. Lactate, renal dysfunction, toxins, vomiting alkalosis, or treatment can add mixed acid-base patterns.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Total-body water and electrolyte depletion with serum shifts
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Osmotic diuresis, vomiting, acidosis, insulin deficiency, renal impairment, and treatment timing create total-body potassium, phosphate, magnesium, sodium, and water deficits while measured serum potassium may be high, normal, or low.
Water-sodium losses, vomiting, poor intake, vasodilation, infection, pancreatitis overlap, or delayed treatment reduce perfusion, raising tachycardia, hypotension, AKI, lactate, and shock hazards.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Neurologic, cardiac, and multiorgan injury cascade
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Severe acidemia, hyperosmolality or rapid osmotic shifts, cerebral edema, coma, seizure, arrhythmia, shock, AKI, respiratory failure, and trigger illness accumulate into near-term mortality risk.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Recovery with effective insulin, fluids, and trigger control
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Adequate insulin, dextrose when needed, volume repletion, electrolyte replacement, and trigger control suppress ketogenesis, close the anion gap, restore perfusion, and reduce event hazards.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Loss of effective insulin permits unchecked lipolysis and hepatic ketone production.
Insulin deficiency increases hepatic glucose output and reduces peripheral glucose disposal.
Stress hormones amplify glucagon-driven lipolysis and ketogenesis.
Counter-regulatory stress raises hepatic glucose output and insulin resistance.
Ketoacid accumulation creates high anion-gap acidemia.
Glucosuria and osmotic diuresis deplete water, sodium, potassium, phosphate, and magnesium.
Osmotic diuresis and vomiting reduce intravascular volume.
Severe acidemia worsens mental status, cardiac stability, and respiratory work.
Shock and hypoperfusion propagate organ injury.
Insulin deficiency usually raises glucose, though euglycemic contexts can blunt this axis.
Hyperglycemia is a common expression of the osmotic-diuresis mechanism.
Beta-hydroxybutyrate is the dominant circulating ketoacid in DKA.
Clinical blood ketone positivity tracks ketogenesis.
Ketonuria is common, though beta-hydroxybutyrate may be underestimated by nitroprusside urine tests.
Accumulated ketoacid anions widen the anion gap.
Buffering of ketoacids lowers bicarbonate.
Ketoacid burden lowers arterial or venous pH.
Metabolic acid burden lowers base excess.
Respiratory compensation lowers PaCO2 through hyperventilation.
Metabolic acidosis drives tachypnea.
Deep Kussmaul breathing is a clinical expression of severe metabolic acidosis.
Glucosuria causes osmotic polyuria.
Water loss and hyperosmolality cause thirst.
Catabolism and fluid loss cause weight loss, especially in new-onset diabetes.
Measured sodium is often low from translocational dilution, though true or corrected hypernatremia may occur.
Total-body potassium depletion may present as low serum potassium; acidosis and renal dysfunction may mask it.
Hyperglycemia and water loss raise effective osmolality.
Osmotic diuresis and vomiting cause clinical dehydration.
Hypovolemia, acidosis, infection, and stress produce tachycardia.
Severe fluid deficit and shock lower perfusion pressure.
Prerenal azotemia and catabolism raise BUN.
Hypoperfusion and AKI raise creatinine.
Shock, catecholamines, and altered metabolism can raise lactate in severe DKA.
Stress leukocytosis can occur with or without infection.
Acidemia and gastric dysmotility commonly cause nausea and vomiting.
DKA can cause abdominal pain independent of pancreatitis or surgical abdomen.
Hyperosmolality, acidemia, dehydration, cerebral edema, and trigger illness can alter mental status.
Very severe DKA can present with coma.
Seizures can occur with severe acidemia, osmotic disturbance, cerebral edema, or comorbid neurologic stress.
Severe hypovolemia and trigger illness can cause shock.
Potassium and phosphate derangements, acidemia, and treatment shifts can provoke arrhythmia.
Children and severe hyperosmolar DKA are vulnerable to cerebral edema during disease and correction.
Hypoperfusion and rhabdomyolysis or shock overlap can cause AKI.
Severe respiratory compensation can fatigue; coma or trigger infection can require ventilation.
Death emerges through cerebral edema, shock, arrhythmia, respiratory failure, AKI, trigger illness, and delayed correction.
Shock is a major near-term death pathway in severe DKA.
Arrhythmia from potassium, phosphate, or severe acidemia can be fatal.
Cerebral edema is a feared pediatric DKA death pathway.

axes.shape_free_text: Known diabetes mellitus, insulin dependence, prior DKA, or established diabetes care context.
Presentation suggests previously undiagnosed diabetes with prodromal polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, high HbA1c, or new insulin requirement.
Missed insulin, pump failure, inadequate insulin, medication nonadherence, or interruption of basal insulin context.
Recent sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitor exposure that can promote euglycemic or lower-glucose DKA physiology.
Recent fasting, surgery, poor carbohydrate intake, low-carbohydrate diet, vomiting, pregnancy nausea, or perioperative stress context that can lower glucose while permitting ketogenesis.
Clinical or microbiologic context of infection acting as a DKA trigger; trigger confirmation should remain context or confirmatory evidence, not disease-name scope.
Serum or plasma glucose. Usually high in DKA but may be below 250 mg/dL in SGLT2-inhibitor, fasting, pregnancy, partial insulin treatment, or postoperative euglycemic contexts.
Chronic glycemia context; often high in undiagnosed or uncontrolled diabetes but can be near normal in acute SGLT2 or rare fulminant contexts.
Serum beta-hydroxybutyrate concentration; principal ketone body in DKA.
Positive blood ketone or ketone bodies when reported semi-quantitatively.
Ketonuria on urine dipstick; can be strong in DKA but may lag beta-hydroxybutyrate state.
Anion gap widened by ketoacids, with lactate, renal failure, toxins, or albumin correction as additional context.
Serum bicarbonate or total CO2; low in DKA acidemia but may be partly masked by vomiting alkalosis or therapy.
Arterial or venous pH; low in DKA, with venous and arterial values consumed as the same acidemia axis for PoC ranking.
Base excess/base deficit; negative values reflect metabolic acid burden.
Arterial or venous CO2 tension; typically low from respiratory compensation unless respiratory failure supervenes.
Lactate may be normal or elevated from hypoperfusion, catecholamines, severe DKA metabolism, sepsis, seizure, or shock.
Measured or effective serum osmolality; high with hyperglycemia, water deficit, and DKA-HHS overlap.
Measured sodium; can be low from hyperglycemic water shift, normal, or high when free water loss dominates.
Sodium corrected for hyperglycemia; high values indicate severe free-water deficit.
Measured potassium can be high, normal, or profoundly low despite total-body depletion; initial low potassium is critical for treatment vector behavior.
Chloride is variable at presentation and can rise with saline therapy or mixed hyperchloremic acidosis.
Measured phosphate may be normal initially and fall during insulin treatment; severe low values can cause weakness, respiratory failure, or arrhythmia.
BUN rises with dehydration, AKI, catabolism, and shock.
Creatinine rises with dehydration, AKI, baseline kidney disease, and assay interference in severe ketonemia.
Stress leukocytosis is common; infection can further increase or modify this axis.
CRP is often normal or mildly high in uncomplicated DKA and rises with infection, pancreatitis, or inflammatory trigger context.
Heart rate increased by dehydration, acidosis, infection, pain, stress, or shock.
Respiratory rate rises with metabolic acidosis; Kussmaul breathing is the deep breathing pattern satellite.
Deep, labored Kussmaul breathing from severe metabolic acidosis.
Systolic pressure may be preserved or low; severe DKA with hypovolemia or trigger illness can shock.
Perfusion pressure; falls with severe hypovolemia, vasodilation, shock, or sedative/critical-care context.
Temperature may be normal; fever suggests infection or inflammatory trigger and hypothermia can occur in severe shock.
Oxygen saturation is often preserved but can fall with pneumonia, ARDS, shock, aspiration, or altered mental status.
Dry mucosa, poor skin turgor, delayed capillary refill, weak pulses, oliguria, or clinical volume depletion.
Polyuria, nocturia, or high urine output before volume collapse.
Excessive thirst or increased fluid intake from osmotic diuresis.
Unintentional weight loss from catabolism and osmotic diuresis, especially in new-onset diabetes.
Nausea, vomiting, retching, anorexia, or poor oral intake during DKA.
Abdominal pain can be DKA-related, pancreatitis overlap, or mimic context.
Fatigue, tiredness, weakness, malaise, or reduced energy before or during DKA.
Confusion, drowsiness, obtundation, agitation, delirium, decreased consciousness, or coma spectrum.
Coma or unresponsiveness from severe DKA physiology or complications.
Observed seizure during severe acidemia, osmotic disturbance, cerebral edema concern, or comorbid neurologic stress.
Shock, circulatory collapse, or arrest hazard from severe hypovolemia, acidemia, trigger illness, or pancreatitis overlap.
AKI hazard from hypovolemia, shock, rhabdomyolysis, hyperosmolality, infection, or nephrotoxic context.
Arrhythmia hazard from potassium, phosphate, magnesium, acidemia, catecholamines, or treatment shifts.
Cerebral edema or osmotic brain injury hazard, especially in pediatric severe DKA or rapid osmotic shifts.
Need for airway or ventilation from coma, respiratory fatigue, pneumonia, ARDS, shock, or severe acidemia.
Lifespan outcome hazard for DKA, emerging from shock, cerebral edema, severe acidemia, arrhythmia, AKI, respiratory failure, trigger illness, delayed insulin/fluids, and host reserve.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Ketoacid anions widen the anion gap.
High anion gap and bicarbonate depletion track the same acid load.
Bicarbonate and pH fall together in metabolic acidosis.
Severe acidemia destabilizes myocardium and potassium physiology.
Both severe hypo- and hyperkalemia raise arrhythmia risk.
Glucose is a major contributor to effective osmolality.
Hypoperfusion raises lactate, although DKA metabolism can contribute independently.
Life-threatening arrhythmia is an immediate death pathway.
Cerebral edema strongly increases DKA mortality.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Hypernatremic or hyperosmolar DKA requires controlled correction rather than blind hypotonic fluid.
Pulmonary edema or cardiac disease narrows the safe resuscitation window.

treatments.context_specific_role: Restores intravascular volume and renal perfusion while insulin and electrolyte vectors close ketoacidosis.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Insulin shifts potassium intracellularly and can be dangerous when initial potassium is very low.
Euglycemic DKA still requires insulin to suppress ketogenesis despite lower glucose.

treatments.context_specific_role: Suppresses ketogenesis and closes the anion gap; glucose lowering alone is not the endpoint.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Dextrose becomes useful when glucose is low enough that insulin continuation would otherwise be unsafe.

treatments.context_specific_role: Allows insulin to continue until ketosis resolves in euglycemic or falling-glucose DKA.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Measured hyperkalemia can coexist with total-body deficit but immediate replacement must respect arrhythmia risk.

treatments.context_specific_role: Controls potassium trajectory so insulin can be delivered without provoking lethal hypokalemia.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Phosphate replacement can worsen hypocalcemia or calcium-phosphate precipitation risk.

treatments.context_specific_role: Addresses severe or symptomatic phosphate depletion as a complication vector rather than a DKA diagnosis label.
Reduces stress-hormone drive when a real trigger is active; agent choice belongs to the infection or source-control context.

sigma_modulation.clinical_rationale: ICU monitoring and rescue reduce uncontrolled volatility.

treatments.context_specific_role: Contains lethal complication vectors while metabolic treatment closes the ketoacidosis.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Known insulin-dependent diabetes directly raises diabetes-context evidence.
Absolute insulin deficiency often causes marked hyperglycemia.
Prodromal osmotic symptoms and high HbA1c identify new diabetes context.
New-onset diabetes often has days to weeks of osmotic symptoms.
Catabolism and fluid loss precede presentation.
Observed SGLT2 inhibitor exposure directly raises this context axis.
SGLT2 glycosuria can make DKA euglycemic or lower-glucose.
SGLT2 context can promote ketogenesis with lower glucose.

treatment_effect_modulation.dextrose_containing_fluid_support_when_g: stronger because insulin must continue despite lower glucose

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Observed fasting or surgical stress raises this context axis.
Reduced carbohydrate intake can lower glucose while ketogenesis continues.
Observed infection context raises stress-hormone drive.
Infection can add leukocytosis to stress leukocytosis.
Infection may add fever.

treatment_effect_modulation.trigger_control_for_infection_or_intercu: stronger when infection context is active

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Children and adolescents have higher cerebral edema vulnerability in severe DKA.
Pediatric mortality is low with timely care but cerebral edema is a distinctive severe-risk pathway.
Baseline kidney disease raises creatinine background.
Reduced renal potassium excretion changes potassium expression.
Lower renal reserve raises AKI risk.
Pregnancy can develop DKA at lower glucose with accelerated starvation physiology.
Pregnancy increases ketogenesis vulnerability.

supportive_care: Track the disease by ketoacid closure, not glucose alone: beta-hydroxybutyrate, anion gap, bicarbonate, pH, and clinical perfusion should move together under effective therapy.
Do not exclude DKA when glucose is below 250 mg/dL if ketosis and anion-gap acidosis are present; SGLT2 inhibitors, fasting, surgery, pregnancy, and partial insulin exposure can blunt hyperglycemia.
Do not turn euglycemic DKA, HHS overlap, pancreatitis-associated DKA, starvation ketosis, alcoholic ketoacidosis, or infection-triggered DKA into first-layer disease-name qualifiers.

Preserve presentation evidence even when it overlaps mimics: abdominal pain, leukocytosis, lactate elevation, shock, pancreatitis labs, and COVID or infection context should remain structured rather than deleted.

Keep final diabetes classification, trigger confirmation, microbiology, imaging-only trigger workup, treatment response, and outcome in confirmatory or non-ranking sections unless a post-workup diagnostic mode explicitly uses them.
Treatment complications such as hypokalemia, hypophosphatemia, cerebral edema, hypoglycemia, or fluid overload should enter through event hazards or course observations, not as diagnostic labels.
